title: Σίτου καὶ οἴνοιο
titleEn: Odysseus Pleads for a Meal — Iliad 19.154–237
source: Homer, The Iliad, Greek text of D. B. Monro and T. W. Allen, Homeri Opera, tomi I–II, 3rd ed. (Oxford Classical Texts; Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1920), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg001.perseus-grc2, sha256 ae8b617018c6e5af. Text as printed: the edition sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Odysseus answers Achilles' demand to fight at once: an army that has not eaten cannot fight all day, and the dead cannot be mourned with an empty belly. He asks that the people be sent to eat, the gifts shown before all, and Agamemnon swear that he never touched Briseis, then make amends with a feast. Agamemnon agrees to swear, asks Achilles to wait, and orders the gifts, the women and a boar brought. Achilles refuses food while Patroclus lies dead. Odysseus replies that he is older and knows more: men tire of fighting quickly, the dead must be buried after one day of tears, and the living must eat so that they can fight on. He ends with a call to go out together against the Trojans.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη πολύμητις Ὀδυσσεύς·
sentences.tr: ton d’ apameibomenos prosephē polymētis Odysseus·
sentences.l: Him answering addressed many-wiled Odysseus:
sentences.i: In answer Odysseus of many wiles said to him:
sentences.n: Odysseus answers Achilles, who has just called for the army to fight at once; the speech that follows asks that the men eat first. The line is a stock reply-formula that recurs often. ἀπαμειβόμενος is a participle, ‘answering’, and προσέφη is the past tense of προσφημί, ‘addressed’. πολύμητις ‘many-wiled’ is Odysseus’ stock epithet, translated every time.

sentences.t:
μὴ δ’ οὕτως, ἀγαθός περ ἐών, θεοείκελ’ Ἀχιλλεῦ
νήστιας ὄτρυνε προτὶ Ἴλιον υἷας Ἀχαιῶν
Τρωσὶ μαχησομένους,
sentences.tr:
mē d’ houtōs, agathos per eōn, theoeikel’ Achilleu
nēstias otryne proti Ilion huias Achaiōn
Trōsi machēsomenous,
sentences.l:
“Not so, though you are good, god-resembling Achilles,
fasting do not urge on towards Ilium the sons of the Achaeans
to fight the Trojans,
sentences.i: “Do not, Achilles, you who are like a god, good as you are, urge the sons of the Achaeans on to Ilium fasting, to fight the Trojans,
sentences.n: Odysseus begins with a prohibition: μή with the present imperative ὄτρυνε means ‘do not urge on’, an act now being pressed. μὴ δ’ οὕτως ‘not so’ is explained by the next word, νήστιας ‘fasting’. ἀγαθός περ ἐών is ‘good though you are’: ἀγαθός means good at what a man does, and here it means good in battle. θεοείκελ’ Ἀχιλλεῦ ‘god-resembling’ is a stock address, translated every time. μαχησομένους is a future participle of purpose, ‘to fight’. The edition prints no comma after Ἀχιλλεῦ.

sentences.t:
ἐπεὶ οὐκ ὀλίγον χρόνον ἔσται
φύλοπις, εὖτ’ ἂν πρῶτον ὁμιλήσωσι φάλαγγες
ἀνδρῶν, ἐν δὲ θεὸς πνεύσῃ μένος ἀμφοτέροισιν.
sentences.tr:
epei ouk oligon chronon estai
phylopis, eut’ an prōton homilēsōsi phalanges
andrōn, en de theos pneusēi menos amphoteroisin.
sentences.l:
since not for a short time will there be
battle-din, when first the battle-lines mingle
of men, and a god breathes in might upon both sides.
sentences.i: since the din of battle will last no short time, whenever the battle-lines of men first close and a god breathes might into both sides.
sentences.n: This unit begins in the middle of line 157. Odysseus gives his reason: the fighting will be long, so the men will need strength. χρόνον ‘time’ is an accusative of duration, ‘for a time’. φύλοπις ‘battle-din’ is the house rendering; εὖτ’ ἂν … ὁμιλήσωσι is a general ‘whenever’ clause with the aorist subjunctive, ‘mingle’, i.e. come together. In ἐν … πνεύσῃ the preverb ἐν stands apart from its verb (tmesis): ‘breathe into’. μένος is ‘might’, the force a god can put into a man.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ πάσασθαι ἄνωχθι θοῇς ἐπὶ νηυσὶν Ἀχαιοὺς
σίτου καὶ οἴνοιο·
sentences.tr:
alla pasasthai anōchthi thoēis epi nēusin Achaious
sitou kai oinoio·
sentences.l:
But bid the Achaeans taste, beside the swift ships,
of food and of wine;
sentences.i: Instead, bid the Achaeans take food and wine beside the swift ships;
sentences.n: Odysseus now gives the remedy: let the army eat. ἄνωχθι is the imperative of ἄνωγα ‘bid’, a perfect with present sense. πάσασθαι is the aorist infinitive of πατέομαι ‘eat, taste’, and it takes the genitive σίτου καὶ οἴνοιο ‘of food and wine’, because it names the stuff a man partakes of. θοῇς … νηυσίν is the epic dative plural, ‘swift ships’.

sentences.t: τὸ γὰρ μένος ἐστὶ καὶ ἀλκή.
sentences.tr: to gar menos esti kai alkē.
sentences.l: for that is strength and might;
sentences.i: for that is strength and might;
sentences.n: τὸ γάρ ‘for that’ means the food and wine. Two words for fighting power stand together, μένος and ἀλκή. The line stands in the same words at 9.706 and keeps its English there, ‘strength and might’: μένος is ‘might’ elsewhere (as in line 159), but here, as there, it is ‘strength’ so that the pair stays two words in English. This unit begins in the middle of line 161.

sentences.t:
οὐ γὰρ ἀνὴρ πρόπαν ἦμαρ ἐς ἠέλιον καταδύντα
ἄκμηνος σίτοιο δυνήσεται ἄντα μάχεσθαι·
sentences.tr:
ou gar anēr propan ēmar es ēelion katadynta
akmēnos sitoio dynēsetai anta machesthai·
sentences.l:
for not a man the whole day until the sun setting
unfed of food will be able to fight face to face;
sentences.i: For no man, without food, will be able to fight face to face the whole day through until the sun goes down;
sentences.n: ἐς ἠέλιον καταδύντα is ‘until the setting sun’, with ἐς in the sense of ‘up to’. ἄκμηνος ‘unfed’ takes σίτοιο in the genitive, ‘unfed of food’, a genitive of what is lacking. δυνήσεται is the future of δύναμαι, ‘will be able’. ἄντα is the adverb ‘face to face’.

sentences.t:
εἴ περ γὰρ θυμῷ γε μενοινάᾳ πολεμίζειν,
ἀλλά τε λάθρῃ γυῖα βαρύνεται, ἠδὲ κιχάνει
δίψά τε καὶ λιμός, βλάβεται δέ τε γούνατ’ ἰόντι.
sentences.tr:
ei per gar thymōi ge menoinaāi polemizein,
alla te lathrēi guia barynetai, ēde kichanei
dipsa te kai limos, blabetai de te gounat’ ionti.
sentences.i: For even if he is eager in his heart to make war, his limbs grow heavy without his knowing it, thirst and hunger come upon him, and his knees are hampered as he goes.
sentences.n: This unit sets out what hunger does to a fighter. εἴ περ … μενοινάᾳ is ‘even if he is minded’, a subjunctive from μενοινάω, with the uncontracted ending -άᾳ (Attic -ᾷ). θυμῷ γε ‘in his heart’ gives the place where the will is. λάθρῃ means ‘secretly, without his noticing’. κιχάνει ‘comes upon’ has two subjects, δίψα and λιμός, ‘thirst’ and ‘hunger’. βλάβεται is the passive of βλάπτω, here ‘be hampered, disabled’, and ἰόντι is a dative participle, ‘as he goes’, that says whom it happens to. The τε in several of these clauses is the epic τε of general statements.

sentences.t:
ὃς δέ κ’ ἀνὴρ οἴνοιο κορεσσάμενος καὶ ἐδωδῆς
ἀνδράσι δυσμενέεσσι πανημέριος πολεμίζῃ,
θαρσαλέον νύ οἱ ἦτορ ἐνὶ φρεσίν, οὐδέ τι γυῖα
πρὶν κάμνει πρὶν πάντας ἐρωῆσαι πολέμοιο.
sentences.tr:
hos de k’ anēr oinoio koressamenos kai edōdēs
andrasi dysmeneessi panēmerios polemizēi,
tharsaleon ny hoi ētor eni phresin, oude ti guia
prin kamnei prin pantas erōēsai polemoio.
sentences.l:
But the man who, having had his fill of wine and of food,
fights all day long against ill-disposed men,
bold is his heart within his wits, and his limbs
sooner do not tire at all, before all have held back from war.
sentences.i: But the man who has had his fill of wine and food and fights all day against ill-disposed men has a bold heart in his mind, and his limbs do not tire at all before every man has held back from the war.
sentences.n: This is the other half of the argument: the fed man. ὃς δέ κ’ ἀνήρ … πολεμίζῃ is a general relative clause with the subjunctive, ‘whoever fights’. κορεσσάμενος is the aorist middle participle of κορέννυμι, ‘having had his fill’, and takes the genitive. δυσμενέεσσι is the epic dative plural of δυσμενής ‘ill-disposed’, here simply ‘enemies’. θαρσαλέον ‘bold’ stands first as the predicate of ἦτορ. In πρὶν κάμνει πρὶν … the first πρίν is an adverb, ‘sooner’, and the second a conjunction, ‘before’. ἐρωῆσαι is an aorist infinitive that means ‘to hold back’, here from the war.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄγε λαὸν μὲν σκέδασον καὶ δεῖπνον ἄνωχθι
ὅπλεσθαι·
sentences.tr:
all’ age laon men skedason kai deipnon anōchthi
hoplesthai·
sentences.l:
But come, the people disperse, and a meal bid
them prepare;
sentences.i: But come: send the people away, and bid them prepare a meal;
sentences.n: Odysseus turns from argument to orders, and the orders have a sequence: dismiss the troops to eat, then bring the gifts. ἀλλ’ ἄγε is ‘but come’, the call to act. σκέδασον is the aorist imperative of σκεδάννυμι ‘scatter’, here to break up the assembly. δεῖπνον is ‘a meal’. ὅπλεσθαι is the infinitive of ὁπλίζομαι ‘make ready’, here after ἄνωχθι ‘bid’; the unspoken object is the people.

sentences.t:
τὰ δὲ δῶρα ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν Ἀγαμέμνων
οἰσέτω ἐς μέσσην ἀγορήν, ἵνα πάντες Ἀχαιοὶ
ὀφθαλμοῖσιν ἴδωσι, σὺ δὲ φρεσὶ σῇσιν ἰανθῇς.
sentences.tr:
ta de dōra anax andrōn Agamemnōn
oisetō es messēn agorēn, hina pantes Achaioi
ophthalmoisin idōsi, sy de phresi sēisin ianthēis.
sentences.l:
and the gifts, lord of men, Agamemnon
let him bring into the middle of the assembly, so that all the Achaeans
may see with their eyes, and you in your wits be gladdened.
sentences.i: and let Agamemnon, lord of men, bring the gifts into the middle of the assembly, so that all the Achaeans may see them with their own eyes and your mind be gladdened.
sentences.n: This unit begins in the middle of line 172. Odysseus wants the gifts shown in public, in front of the whole army: the payment is also a public acknowledgment. τὰ … δῶρα is the object of οἰσέτω, the 3rd person imperative of φέρω ‘let him bring’. ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν ‘lord of men’ is Agamemnon’s stock title. ἐς μέσσην ἀγορήν is ‘into the middle of the assembly’. ἵνα with the subjunctives ἴδωσι and ἰανθῇς is a purpose clause; ἰανθῇς is the aorist passive of ἰαίνω ‘warm, cheer’. ὀφθαλμοῖσιν and φρεσὶ σῇσιν are epic datives.

sentences.t:
ὀμνυέτω δέ τοι ὅρκον ἐν Ἀργείοισιν ἀναστὰς
μή ποτε τῆς εὐνῆς ἐπιβήμεναι ἠδὲ μιγῆναι·
sentences.tr:
omnyetō de toi horkon en Argeioisin anastas
mē pote tēs eunēs epibēmenai ēde migēnai·
sentences.l:
And let him swear an oath to you, rising up among the Argives,
never to have set foot upon her bed, nor to have mingled with her;
sentences.i: And let him rise among the Argives and swear you an oath that he never mounted her bed or lay with her;
sentences.n: Odysseus now sets out the oath that Agamemnon must swear: that he has not touched Briseis, the captive woman who is the cause of the quarrel. She is not named here; ‘her’ in the line is the girl whom the oath is about. ὀμνυέτω is the 3rd person imperative of ὄμνυμι ‘swear’; τοι is the epic form of σοι, ‘to you’. ἀναστάς is ‘having risen’, because an oath is sworn standing. μή ποτε with the infinitives ἐπιβήμεναι and μιγῆναι gives the content of the oath, ‘never to have…’. ἐπιβήμεναι is an epic infinitive of ἐπιβαίνω ‘set foot on, mount’, and μιγῆναι the aorist passive of μίγνυμι ‘mingle’, both sexual. Line 176 stands in the same words elsewhere in the poem.

sentences.t: ἣ θέμις ἐστὶν ἄναξ ἤ τ’ ἀνδρῶν ἤ τε γυναικῶν·
sentences.tr: hē themis estin anax ē t’ andrōn ē te gynaikōn·
sentences.l: as is the custom, lord, whether of men or of women;
sentences.i: as is the custom, lord, whether of men or of women;
sentences.n: ἣ θέμις ἐστίν ‘as is the custom’ says that this is the usual form of such an oath. θέμις is custom or established right, not written law. ἄναξ is most naturally a vocative, ‘lord’, addressed to Achilles, not Agamemnon; the edition prints no commas, so a reader may also take it with the genitives. ἤ τ’ … ἤ τε ‘whether … or’ says the custom holds between men and women alike.

sentences.t: καὶ δὲ σοὶ αὐτῷ θυμὸς ἐνὶ φρεσὶν ἵλαος ἔστω.
sentences.tr: kai de soi autōi thymos eni phresin hilaos estō.
sentences.l: And moreover for you yourself let the heart in your wits be gracious.
sentences.i: And you yourself, too, let the heart in your mind be gracious.
sentences.n: Odysseus now asks something of Achilles: that he accept the oath in a gracious spirit. καὶ δέ ‘and moreover’ adds a second point. σοὶ αὐτῷ ‘you yourself’ turns from Agamemnon to Achilles. ἵλαος ‘gracious’ is the word for a god or a man who is willing to be won over. ἔστω is the 3rd person imperative of εἰμί, ‘let it be’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἔπειτά σε δαιτὶ ἐνὶ κλισίῃς ἀρεσάσθω
πιείρῃ, ἵνα μή τι δίκης ἐπιδευὲς ἔχῃσθα.
sentences.tr:
autar epeita se daiti eni klisiēis aresasthō
pieirēi, hina mē ti dikēs epideues echēistha.
sentences.l:
But thereafter let him appease you with a feast
in the huts, a rich one, so that of justice nothing lacking you may have.
sentences.i: And afterwards let him make amends to you with a rich feast in the huts, so that you may lack nothing of what is just.
sentences.n: Agamemnon is the subject of ἀρεσάσθω, though he is not named in this sentence. The feast is the second half of the amends. ἀρεσάσθω is the aorist imperative middle of ἀρέσκω, ‘make amends to, satisfy’. δαιτί ‘with a feast’ is the means. κλισίῃς is the epic dative plural, ‘in the huts’, governed by ἐνί; κλισίη is ‘hut’. πιείρῃ ‘rich’ qualifies δαιτί. ἵνα μή τι δίκης ἐπιδευὲς ἔχῃσθα is a purpose clause, with δίκης ‘of what is due’ governed by ἐπιδευές ‘lacking’; ἔχῃσθα is the subjunctive ἔχῃς with the epic ending -σθα.

sentences.t:
Ἀτρεΐδη σὺ δ’ ἔπειτα δικαιότερος καὶ ἐπ’ ἄλλῳ
ἔσσεαι.
sentences.tr:
Atreïdē sy d’ epeita dikaioteros kai ep’ allōi
esseai.
sentences.l:
Son of Atreus, and you thereafter more just
even toward another will be.
sentences.i: And you, son of Atreus, will be more just afterwards toward any other man as well.
sentences.n: Odysseus now turns to Agamemnon himself and speaks to him directly, as ‘son of Atreus’. Ἀτρεΐδη is a vocative. δικαιότερος is a comparative, ‘more just’. καὶ ἐπ’ ἄλλῳ ‘even toward another’ means any other man too, not only Achilles. ἔσσεαι is the uncontracted future of εἰμί (Attic ἔσῃ). The sentence ends in the middle of line 182.

sentences.t:
οὐ μὲν γάρ τι νεμεσσητὸν βασιλῆα
ἄνδρ’ ἀπαρέσσασθαι ὅτε τις πρότερος χαλεπήνῃ.
sentences.tr:
ou men gar ti nemessēton basilēa
andr’ aparessasthai hote tis proteros chalepēnēi.
sentences.l:
For not at all a thing to resent is it, a king
a man to appease, whenever someone first has grown harsh.”
sentences.i: For it is not at all a thing to resent that a king should make amends to a man, whenever someone has been the first to be harsh.”
sentences.n: This unit begins in the middle of line 182. Odysseus gives the principle: a king loses nothing by making amends. νεμεσσητόν ‘a thing to resent’ is the house rendering, and βασιλῆα ἄνδρ’ ἀπαρέσσασθαι is an accusative and infinitive, ‘that a king should appease a man’. ἀπαρέσσασθαι is the same verb as ἀρεσάσθω above, with the prefix ἀπ-, ‘make amends to’. τις is ‘someone’, the first to be harsh; the Greek does not name him, but in this setting the one who began the quarrel is the king. χαλεπήνῃ is the aorist subjunctive of χαλεπαίνω ‘grow harsh’, i.e. be angry, in a general ‘whenever’ clause. Odysseus’ speech ends here.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπεν ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν Ἀγαμέμνων·
sentences.tr: ton d’ aute proseeipen anax andrōn Agamemnōn·
sentences.l: Him then in turn addressed the lord of men, Agamemnon:
sentences.i: Then Agamemnon, lord of men, spoke to him in turn:
sentences.n: Agamemnon answers. The line is a stock speech-introduction, and here the ‘him’ (τόν) is Odysseus. προσέειπεν is the epic aorist of προσεῖπον, ‘addressed’, and αὖτε ‘in turn’ marks the change of speaker. ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν ‘lord of men’ is his stock title, translated every time.

sentences.t: χαίρω σεῦ Λαερτιάδη τὸν μῦθον ἀκούσας·
sentences.tr: chairō seu Laertiadē ton mython akousas·
sentences.l: “I rejoice at you, Laertes’-son, having heard the word;
sentences.i: “Son of Laertes, I am glad of you, having heard your speech;
sentences.n: Agamemnon begins by approving what Odysseus has said. χαίρω σεῦ is ‘I rejoice at you’, with the genitive of the person who is the cause; σεῦ is the epic form of σοῦ. Λαερτιάδη is a patronymic vocative, ‘son of Laertes’, like Ἀτρεΐδη. τὸν μῦθον ἀκούσας is ‘having heard the word’; μῦθος here is the speech just made.

sentences.t: ἐν μοίρῃ γὰρ πάντα διίκεο καὶ κατέλεξας.
sentences.tr: en moirēi gar panta diikeo kai katelexas.
sentences.l: for in due portion everything you have gone through and told over.
sentences.i: for you have gone through everything and set it out as was due.
sentences.n: ἐν μοίρῃ ‘in due portion’ means ‘as was due, in the right measure’, the house rendering of the phrase. διίκεο is a 2nd person aorist middle of διικνέομαι ‘go through’ with the uncontracted ending -εο (Attic -ου). κατέλεξας is the aorist of καταλέγω, ‘recount, set out in order’.

sentences.t:
ταῦτα δ’ ἐγὼν ἐθέλω ὀμόσαι, κέλεται δέ με θυμός,
οὐδ’ ἐπιορκήσω πρὸς δαίμονος.
sentences.tr:
tauta d’ egōn ethelō omosai, keletai de me thymos,
oud’ epiorkēsō pros daimonos.
sentences.l:
And these things I am willing to swear, and my heart bids me,
and I shall not swear falsely before a divinity.
sentences.i: I am willing to swear to this, and my heart bids me; I shall not swear falsely before a divinity.
sentences.n: Agamemnon accepts the oath. ὀμόσαι is the aorist infinitive of ὄμνυμι ‘swear’; ἐθέλω ‘am willing’ governs it. κέλεται ‘bids’ has θυμός as its subject. ἐπιορκήσω is the future of ἐπιορκέω ‘swear falsely’, from ἐπίορκος ‘false oath’. πρὸς δαίμονος is ‘before, in the presence of, a divinity’: πρός with the genitive is the form of an oath. δαίμων is a divine power, left unnamed. The unit ends in the middle of line 188.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ Ἀχιλλεὺς
μιμνέτω αὐτόθι τεῖος ἐπειγόμενός περ Ἄρηος·
sentences.tr:
autar Achilleus
mimnetō autothi teios epeigomenos per Arēos·
sentences.l:
but Achilles
let him stay right here for a while, though pressing on to Ares;
sentences.i: but let Achilles stay here for the time being, eager as he is for battle;
sentences.n: This unit begins in the middle of line 188. αὐτάρ ‘but’ turns to Achilles, who wants to fight at once. μιμνέτω is the 3rd person imperative of μίμνω ‘stay’. αὐτόθι ‘right here’ ends in -θι, the suffix of place. τεῖος means ‘for the time being, meanwhile’. ἐπειγόμενος ‘pressing on’ takes the genitive Ἄρηος, ‘pressing on to Ares’, i.e. eager for the fight: Ares stands for the war itself, and l keeps the god’s name. περ ‘though’ is concessive.

sentences.t:
μίμνετε δ’ ἄλλοι πάντες ἀολλέες, ὄφρά κε δῶρα
ἐκ κλισίης ἔλθῃσι καὶ ὅρκια πιστὰ τάμωμεν.
sentences.tr:
mimnete d’ alloi pantes aollees, ophra ke dōra
ek klisiēs elthēisi kai horkia pista tamōmen.
sentences.l:
and you others all stay, in a close mass, until the gifts
come from the hut and we cut faithful oaths.
sentences.i: and all the rest of you stay together, in a close mass, until the gifts come from the hut and we swear faithful oaths.
sentences.n: Now Agamemnon speaks to the other leaders. μίμνετε is a plural imperative, ‘stay’. ἀολλέες ‘in a close mass’ is the house rendering. ὄφρα κε with the aorist subjunctives ἔλθῃσι and τάμωμεν is ‘until they come’ and ‘until we cut’. The stock phrase ὅρκια τάμνειν, ‘cut oaths’, is the Greek way to say ‘swear an oath with a sacrifice’, because a victim was cut. ἐκ κλισίης ‘from the hut’ is Agamemnon’s hut.

sentences.t: σοὶ δ’ αὐτῷ τόδ’ ἐγὼν ἐπιτέλλομαι ἠδὲ κελεύω·
sentences.tr: soi d’ autōi tod’ egōn epitellomai ēde keleuō·
sentences.l: And to you yourself this I give in charge and bid:
sentences.i: And to you yourself I give this charge and this command:
sentences.n: σοί … αὐτῷ ‘to you yourself’ turns to Odysseus. ἐπιτέλλομαι ‘I give charge’ and κελεύω ‘I bid’ are two verbs of command put together for weight. ἐγών is the epic form of ἐγώ. τόδε ‘this’ points forward to the orders in the next sentence, which is in the infinitive.

sentences.t:
κρινάμενος κούρητας ἀριστῆας Παναχαιῶν
δῶρα ἐμῆς παρὰ νηὸς ἐνεικέμεν, ὅσσ’ Ἀχιλῆϊ
χθιζὸν ὑπέστημεν δώσειν, ἀγέμεν τε γυναῖκας.
sentences.tr:
krinamenos kourētas aristēas Panachaiōn
dōra emēs para nēos eneikemen, hoss’ Achilēï
chthizon hypestēmen dōsein, agemen te gynaikas.
sentences.i: Choose out young men, the best of all the Achaeans, to bring the gifts from my ship, all that we promised Achilles yesterday that we would give, and to lead the women.
sentences.n: The orders follow in the infinitive, a construction that Homer uses for commands: ἐνεικέμεν ‘to bring’ and ἀγέμεν ‘to lead’ stand for imperatives, and the sentence must be read as ‘bring them’, not ‘you will bring them’. κρινάμενος is the aorist middle participle of κρίνω ‘choose out’. κούρητας is ‘young men’ (here a common noun). ἀριστῆας Παναχαιῶν is ‘the best men of all the Achaeans’. ὅσσ’ … δώσειν is ‘as many as we promised to give’; ὑπέστημεν is the aorist of ὑφίστημι ‘undertake, promise’. χθιζόν means ‘yesterday’.

sentences.t:
Ταλθύβιος δέ μοι ὦκα κατὰ στρατὸν εὐρὺν Ἀχαιῶν
κάπρον ἑτοιμασάτω ταμέειν Διί τ’ Ἠελίῳ τε.
sentences.tr:
Talthybios de moi ōka kata straton euryn Achaiōn
kapron hetoimasatō tameein Dii t’ Ēeliōi te.
sentences.l:
And let Talthybius for me quickly throughout the wide host of the Achaeans
a boar make ready to cut for Zeus and for the Sun.”
sentences.i: And let Talthybius quickly make ready for me a boar, throughout the wide host of the Achaeans, to slaughter for Zeus and the Sun.”
sentences.n: Talthybius is Agamemnon’s herald. The boar is for the oath-sacrifice, and the victim is dedicated to the two gods who are witnesses, Zeus and the Sun. ἑτοιμασάτω is the 3rd person aorist imperative of ἑτοιμάζω ‘make ready’. κατὰ στρατὸν εὐρὺν Ἀχαιῶν is ‘throughout the wide army of the Achaeans’. ταμέειν is the aorist infinitive of τάμνω ‘cut’, here ‘cut up, slaughter’ the victim. Ἠελίῳ is the Sun, the god Helios.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη πόδας ὠκὺς Ἀχιλλεύς·
sentences.tr: ton d’ apameibomenos prosephē podas ōkys Achilleus·
sentences.l: Him answering addressed swift-in-feet Achilles:
sentences.i: In answer Achilles, swift of foot, said to him:
sentences.n: Achilles replies to Agamemnon. The line is the stock reply-formula, with πόδας ὠκύς ‘swift in feet’, his stock epithet, translated every time.

sentences.t:
Ἀτρεΐδη κύδιστε ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν Ἀγάμεμνον
ἄλλοτέ περ καὶ μᾶλλον ὀφέλλετε ταῦτα πένεσθαι,
ὁππότε τις μεταπαυσωλὴ πολέμοιο γένηται
καὶ μένος οὐ τόσον ᾖσιν ἐνὶ στήθεσσιν ἐμοῖσι.
sentences.tr:
Atreïdē kydiste anax andrōn Agamemnon
allote per kai mallon ophellete tauta penesthai,
hoppote tis metapausōlē polemoio genētai
kai menos ou toson ēisin eni stēthessin emoisi.
sentences.l:
“Atreus’-son, most glorious, lord of men, Agamemnon,
at another time, even rather, you ought to busy yourselves with these things,
whenever there is some pause of war
and the might is not so great within my chest.
sentences.i: “Son of Atreus, most glorious Agamemnon, lord of men, you ought rather to busy yourselves with these things at some other time, whenever there is a pause in the fighting and the might in my chest is not so great.
sentences.n: Achilles rejects the plan to feast first: this is not the moment for it. ὀφέλλετε is the 2nd person plural of the doubled-λ form of ὀφείλω ‘ought’ (not ὀφέλλω ‘increase’), used with the infinitive πένεσθαι ‘to busy oneself with’, here to tend to the meal and the oath. ἄλλοτέ περ καὶ μᾶλλον is ‘at some other time, even rather’. μεταπαυσωλή ‘a pause, a rest’ is a rare noun, and γένηται is an aorist subjunctive. οὐ τόσον ‘not so much’ with ᾖσιν, an epic subjunctive of εἰμί, ‘be’, says that his might will then be less than it is now, at its fullest. στήθεσσιν is the epic dative plural of στῆθος ‘chest’.

sentences.t:
νῦν δ’ οἳ μὲν κέαται δεδαϊγμένοι, οὓς ἐδάμασσεν
Ἕκτωρ Πριαμίδης, ὅτε οἱ Ζεὺς κῦδος ἔδωκεν,
ὑμεῖς δ’ ἐς βρωτὺν ὀτρύνετον·
sentences.tr:
nyn d’ hoi men keatai dedaïgmenoi, hous edamassen
Hektōr Priamidēs, hote hoi Zeus kydos edōken,
hymeis d’ es brōtyn otryneton·
sentences.i: but now those men lie mangled whom Hector, son of Priam, overcame when Zeus gave him glory, and you two urge us on to food;
sentences.n: νῦν δέ ‘but now’ opposes the present to the ‘other time’ of the last unit. οἳ μὲν κέαται is ‘those lie’, where κέαται is the epic 3rd person plural of κεῖμαι ‘lie’. δεδαϊγμένοι is the perfect passive participle of δαΐζω ‘cut up, mangle’. ἐδάμασσεν is the aorist of δαμάζω ‘subdue’. Ἕκτωρ Πριαμίδης ‘Hector, son of Priam’ is the patronymic pattern. Zeus gave Hector the glory: that is why the dead lie there. The μέν clause is answered by ὑμεῖς δέ, and ὀτρύνετον is a dual present, ‘you two urge’ (the dual ending is the same in the imperative, but the sense here is a statement), the object left unspoken, Agamemnon and Odysseus; the reader should hear that Achilles speaks to both of them at once. ἐς βρωτύν is ‘to food, to eating’.

sentences.t:
ἦ τ’ ἂν ἔγωγε
νῦν μὲν ἀνώγοιμι πτολεμίζειν υἷας Ἀχαιῶν
νήστιας ἀκμήνους, ἅμα δ’ ἠελίῳ καταδύντι
τεύξεσθαι μέγα δόρπον, ἐπὴν τεισαίμεθα λώβην.
sentences.tr:
ē t’ an egōge
nyn men anōgoimi ptolemizein huias Achaiōn
nēstias akmēnous, hama d’ ēeliōi katadynti
teuxesthai mega dorpon, epēn teisaimetha lōbēn.
sentences.l:
Truly I at least
would now bid the sons of the Achaeans to fight,
fasting, unfed, and at the setting of the sun
to make a great supper, when we have taken vengeance for the outrage.
sentences.i: I, for my part, would now bid the sons of the Achaeans fight, fasting and unfed, and at the going down of the sun make a great supper, when we have taken vengeance for the outrage.
sentences.n: This unit begins in the middle of line 205. Achilles says what he would do: fight now, eat after. ἦ τ’ ἂν … ἀνώγοιμι is a potential optative, ‘I would bid’, with ἦ τε ‘truly’. πτολεμίζειν is the epic form of πολεμίζειν ‘make war’. νήστιας ἀκμήνους puts two words together, ‘fasting, unfed’. ἅμα δ’ ἠελίῳ καταδύντι is ‘as the sun sets’, ἅμα with a dative participle. δόρπον is the evening meal, ‘supper’. τεισαίμεθα is the aorist middle optative of τίνυμαι ‘exact payment’, not the usual subjunctive after ἐπήν: it follows the mood of the ‘would’ in ἀνώγοιμι. With λώβην, ‘outrage’, it means to take vengeance for the outrage of the dead.

sentences.t:
πρὶν δ’ οὔ πως ἂν ἔμοιγε φίλον κατὰ λαιμὸν ἰείη
οὐ πόσις οὐδὲ βρῶσις ἑταίρου τεθνηῶτος
ὅς μοι ἐνὶ κλισίῃ δεδαϊγμένος ὀξέϊ χαλκῷ
κεῖται ἀνὰ πρόθυρον τετραμμένος,
sentences.tr:
prin d’ ou pōs an emoige philon kata laimon ieiē
ou posis oude brōsis hetairou tethnēōtos
hos moi eni klisiēi dedaïgmenos oxeï chalkōi
keitai ana prothyron tetrammenos,
sentences.l:
But before that in no way for me, at least, would welcome down the throat go
either drink or food, my companion being dead,
who in my hut, mangled by sharp bronze,
lies up along the forecourt, turned about,
sentences.i: But until then no drink or food could go down my throat gladly, now that my companion is dead, who lies in my hut, mangled by sharp bronze, turned about along the forecourt,
sentences.n: Achilles makes his own refusal personal, and the dead companion is Patroclus, who is not named in the speech. πρίν ‘before that’ is an adverb, ‘until then’. ἂν … ἰείη is a potential optative, ‘could go down’, with φίλον ‘dear, welcome’ as a predicate: he could not take it gladly. κατὰ λαιμόν is ‘down the throat’. πόσις is ‘drink’ (a different word from πόσις ‘husband’), and βρῶσις is ‘food’. ἑταίρου τεθνηῶτος is a genitive absolute, ‘my companion being dead’; τεθνηῶτος is the epic perfect participle of θνῄσκω. ὀξέϊ χαλκῷ is ‘with sharp bronze’. ἀνὰ πρόθυρον ‘along the forecourt’: πρόθυρον is the space before a door. τετραμμένος ‘turned’ is a perfect passive participle of τρέπω; the line does not say which way.

sentences.t:
ἀμφὶ δ’ ἑταῖροι
μύρονται·
sentences.tr:
amphi d’ hetairoi
myrontai·
sentences.l:
and around him the companions
mourn;
sentences.i: and the companions mourn around him;
sentences.n: This unit begins in the middle of line 212. ἀμφί ‘around’ is an adverb here, and ἑταῖροι are ‘companions’: the rest of Achilles’ companions. μύρονται is ‘mourn, weep’, a present middle. The stop after it ends the sentence which began at πρὶν δ’ οὔ πως.

sentences.t:
τό μοι οὔ τι μετὰ φρεσὶ ταῦτα μέμηλεν,
ἀλλὰ φόνος τε καὶ αἷμα καὶ ἀργαλέος στόνος ἀνδρῶν.
sentences.tr:
to moi ou ti meta phresi tauta memēlen,
alla phonos te kai haima kai argaleos stonos andrōn.
sentences.l:
therefore not at all these things are a care in my wits,
but slaughter and blood and the grievous groaning of men.”
sentences.i: That is why these things are no concern of mine, but slaughter and blood and the grievous groaning of men.”
sentences.n: This unit begins in the middle of line 213. τό here means ‘therefore’. μοι … μέμηλεν is a perfect of μέλω, ‘is a care to me’; ταῦτα, the food and drink, is its subject. οὔ τι ‘not at all’ strengthens the denial. φρεσίν ‘wits’ is the house rendering. ἀλλά brings in what does matter to him: φόνος ‘slaughter’, αἷμα ‘blood’ and στόνος ‘groaning’. ἀργαλέος ‘grievous’ qualifies στόνος. Achilles’ speech ends here.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη πολύμητις Ὀδυσσεύς·
sentences.tr: ton d’ apameibomenos prosephē polymētis Odysseus·
sentences.l: Him answering addressed many-wiled Odysseus:
sentences.i: In answer Odysseus of many wiles said to him:
sentences.n: Odysseus answers Achilles. The line is the same reply-formula as at the start of this part, with the same epithet, πολύμητις ‘many-wiled’.

sentences.t:
ὦ Ἀχιλεῦ Πηλῆος υἱὲ μέγα φέρτατ’ Ἀχαιῶν,
κρείσσων εἰς ἐμέθεν καὶ φέρτερος οὐκ ὀλίγον περ
ἔγχει, ἐγὼ δέ κε σεῖο νοήματί γε προβαλοίμην
πολλόν, ἐπεὶ πρότερος γενόμην καὶ πλείονα οἶδα.
sentences.tr:
ō Achileu Pēlēos huie mega phertat’ Achaiōn,
kreissōn eis emethen kai pherteros ouk oligon per
enchei, egō de ke seio noēmati ge probaloimēn
pollon, epei proteros genomēn kai pleiona oida.
sentences.l:
“O Achilles, Peleus’ son, by far the best of the Achaeans,
you are stronger than I and better by no small amount
with the spear, but I might surpass you, at least, in thought
by much, since I was born earlier and know more.
sentences.i: “Achilles, son of Peleus, by far the best of the Achaeans, you are stronger than I and better by no little with the spear, but I might surpass you by much in thought, since I was born before you and know more.
sentences.n: Odysseus meets the refusal with a claim to a different kind of excellence: mind against spear. ὦ Ἀχιλεῦ is a vocative with single λ. Πηλῆος υἱέ ‘son of Peleus’ has the epic genitive -ηος. μέγα φέρτατ’ Ἀχαιῶν is ‘by far the best of the Achaeans’. κρείσσων ‘stronger’ and φέρτερος ‘better’ are comparatives governing ἐμέθεν, the epic form of ἐμοῦ, ‘than I’. ἔγχει is a dative of respect, ‘with the spear’. κε … προβαλοίμην is a potential optative; προβάλλομαι with the genitive σεῖο means ‘throw oneself ahead of, surpass’. νοήματι is ‘in thought’. πρότερος γενόμην is ‘I was born earlier’, i.e. he is older.

sentences.t: τώ τοι ἐπιτλήτω κραδίη μύθοισιν ἐμοῖσιν.
sentences.tr: tō toi epitlētō kradiē mythoisin emoisin.
sentences.l: Therefore let your heart endure my words.
sentences.i: So let your heart bear with my words.
sentences.n: τώ is the epic ‘therefore’. τοι is either the dative ‘to you’ or the particle ‘mark you’, and either fits. ἐπιτλήτω is the 3rd person aorist imperative of a verb meaning ‘endure, bear with’; κραδίη ‘heart’ is its subject. The line turns the claim of age into a request: hear me out.

sentences.t:
αἶψά τε φυλόπιδος πέλεται κόρος ἀνθρώποισιν,
ἧς τε πλείστην μὲν καλάμην χθονὶ χαλκὸς ἔχευεν,
ἄμητος δ’ ὀλίγιστος, ἐπὴν κλίνῃσι τάλαντα
Ζεύς, ὅς τ’ ἀνθρώπων ταμίης πολέμοιο τέτυκται.
sentences.tr:
aipsa te phylopidos peletai koros anthrōpoisin,
hēs te pleistēn men kalamēn chthoni chalkos echeuen,
amētos d’ oligistos, epēn klinēisi talanta
Zeus, hos t’ anthrōpōn tamiēs polemoio tetyktai.
sentences.l:
Quickly of battle-din there comes satiety for men,
of which most stalks to the ground the bronze has poured,
and the harvest least, when he tilts the scales,
Zeus, who of men has been made the steward of war.
sentences.i: Quickly there comes a fullness of the din of battle for men, in which the bronze strews the most stalks on the ground and the harvest is smallest, whenever Zeus tilts the scales, Zeus, who has been made the steward of war for men.
sentences.n: Odysseus now argues that men are soon sated with fighting, and he uses the image of a field being reaped. αἶψά τε ‘quickly’ has the epic τε of a general truth, and πέλεται ‘comes to be’ is a present. κόρος is ‘satiety, fullness’, the genitive φυλόπιδος giving the thing of which men have had enough. ἧς … ἔχευεν is a relative clause with ἧς ‘of which’; ἔχευεν is the aorist of χέω ‘pour’, used for what always happens. καλάμη is a ‘stalk’ of grain, here the fallen men, and ἄμητος is the ‘harvest’, what is gathered in: the bronze lays down many stalks but the harvest is small. ἐπὴν κλίνῃσι τάλαντα is ‘when he tilts the scales’, and the scales are Zeus’. The last line is repeated from elsewhere in the poem. ταμίης ‘steward’ is the one who deals things out.

sentences.t: γαστέρι δ’ οὔ πως ἔστι νέκυν πενθῆσαι Ἀχαιούς·
sentences.tr: gasteri d’ ou pōs esti nekyn penthēsai Achaious·
sentences.l: With the belly, in no way is it possible for the Achaeans to mourn a dead man;
sentences.i: The Achaeans cannot mourn a dead man with the belly;
sentences.n: γαστέρι ‘with the belly’ is the dative of means, and the sense is ‘by fasting’: a man cannot mourn the dead by going hungry. οὔ πως ἔστι is ‘there is no way that’, followed by the infinitive πενθῆσαι ‘to mourn’, with the accusative Ἀχαιούς as the subject of the infinitive. νέκυν is a ‘dead man’, the singular standing for any dead man. Odysseus’ point is that mourning is done by living men, who must keep their strength.

sentences.t:
λίην γὰρ πολλοὶ καὶ ἐπήτριμοι ἤματα πάντα
πίπτουσιν·
sentences.tr:
liēn gar polloi kai epētrimoi ēmata panta
piptousin·
sentences.l:
for too many, and close-set, every day
fall;
sentences.i: for far too many fall, close together, every day;
sentences.n: λίην γάρ gives the reason: ‘for too many’. ἐπήτριμοι ‘close-set’ (‘close together’) is used of the dead falling one upon another, so that mourning each one with a fast would never end. ἤματα πάντα is ‘every day’, an accusative of time. πίπτουσιν is the present of πίπτω ‘fall’.

sentences.t: πότε κέν τις ἀναπνεύσειε πόνοιο;
sentences.tr: pote ken tis anapneuseie ponoio;
sentences.l: when could anyone get his breath back from toil?
sentences.i: When could anyone get his breath back from the toil?
sentences.n: This unit begins in the middle of line 227. The question is rhetorical and its answer is ‘never’. ἀναπνεύσειε is an aorist optative of ἀναπνέω ‘breathe again’, with κε, a potential ‘could’. πόνοιο is the epic genitive of πόνος ‘toil’, which the verb takes for what a man gets his breath back from.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ χρὴ τὸν μὲν καταθάπτειν ὅς κε θάνῃσι
νηλέα θυμὸν ἔχοντας ἐπ’ ἤματι δακρύσαντας·
sentences.tr:
alla chrē ton men katathaptein hos ke thanēisi
nēlea thymon echontas ep’ ēmati dakrysantas·
sentences.l:
But it is necessary to bury the one who dies,
having a pitiless heart, having wept for a day;
sentences.i: But we must bury the man who dies, keeping a pitiless heart, when we have wept for a day;
sentences.n: ἀλλά brings in the alternative: bury the dead briefly and go on. χρή ‘it is necessary’ takes the infinitive καταθάπτειν ‘bury’. τὸν μέν … ὅς κε θάνῃσι is ‘the one who dies’, a general relative with the aorist subjunctive. The accusative participles ἔχοντας and δακρύσαντας agree with an unspoken ‘us’. νηλέα ‘pitiless’ is the house rendering; here it means hard-hearted in the sense of not giving way to grief. ἐπ’ ἤματι is ‘for one day’.

sentences.t:
ὅσσοι δ’ ἂν πολέμοιο περὶ στυγεροῖο λίπωνται
μεμνῆσθαι πόσιος καὶ ἐδητύος, ὄφρ’ ἔτι μᾶλλον
ἀνδράσι δυσμενέεσσι μαχώμεθα νωλεμὲς αἰεὶ
ἑσσάμενοι χροῒ χαλκὸν ἀτειρέα.
sentences.tr:
hossoi d’ an polemoio peri stygeroio lipōntai
memnēsthai posios kai edētyos, ophr’ eti mallon
andrasi dysmeneessi machōmetha nōlemes aiei
hessamenoi chroï chalkon ateirea.
sentences.l:
And as many as are left over from hateful war
let remember drink and food, so that still the more
we may fight with ill-disposed men unceasingly, always,
having put on the unwearied bronze upon the skin.
sentences.i: And let all who are left over from the hateful war remember drink and food, so that we may fight the ill-disposed men all the more, without pause, always, with the unwearied bronze on our skin.
sentences.n: This unit has a loose construction: ὅσσοι … λίπωνται is a relative clause ‘as many as are left’, and μεμνῆσθαι is an infinitive that stands for an imperative, ‘let them remember’; it has no main verb of its own. λίπωνται is an aorist subjunctive middle, and περί stands after its noun; its force with λίπωνται is not certain, and ‘left over from the war’ is the likeliest sense (against ‘left in the fighting around it’). στυγεροῖο ‘hateful’ is the house rendering. μεμνῆσθαι takes the genitives πόσιος καὶ ἐδητύος ‘drink and food’. ὄφρ’ ἔτι μᾶλλον … μαχώμεθα is a purpose clause. δυσμενέεσσι ‘ill-disposed’ is as above. νωλεμές ‘unceasingly’ is an adverb. ἑσσάμενοι is the aorist middle participle of ἕννυμι ‘put on’, and χροΐ is the dative of χρώς ‘skin’. ἀτειρέα ‘unwearied’ is the house rendering for the bronze.

sentences.t:
μηδέ τις ἄλλην
λαῶν ὀτρυντὺν ποτιδέγμενος ἰσχαναάσθω·
sentences.tr:
mēde tis allēn
laōn otryntyn potidegmenos ischanaasthō·
sentences.l:
And let no one of the people, awaiting another
urging, hold himself back;
sentences.i: and let no man of the people hold back, waiting for another summons;
sentences.n: This unit begins in the middle of line 233. The sentence is a negative command. μηδέ τις ‘and let no one’ takes the 3rd person imperative ἰσχαναάσθω, from ἰσχανάομαι ‘hold oneself back’, an epic form. λαῶν ‘of the people’ goes with τις. ὀτρυντύς, from ὀτρύνω ‘urge on’, is an ‘urging’, a call to arms; it is a rare word. ποτιδέγμενος is the epic form of προσδεχόμενος ‘waiting for’, with ποτί for πρός.

sentences.t:
ἥδε γὰρ ὀτρυντὺς κακὸν ἔσσεται ὅς κε λίπηται
νηυσὶν ἐπ’ Ἀργείων·
sentences.tr:
hēde gar otryntys kakon essetai hos ke lipētai
nēusin ep’ Argeiōn·
sentences.l:
for this urging will be an evil
to whoever is left behind at the ships of the Argives;
sentences.i: For this summons will be an evil for anyone who is left behind at the ships of the Argives;
sentences.n: ἥδε ‘this here’ points to the call that Odysseus has just forbidden men to wait for. ὀτρυντύς is the same word as in the line before. ὅς κε λίπηται is a general relative with the aorist subjunctive, ‘whoever is left behind’; λίπηται is middle. νηυσὶν ἐπ’ Ἀργείων is ‘at the ships of the Argives’, and Argives is one of the three names of the army, all used for the same people.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἀθρόοι ὁρμηθέντες
Τρωσὶν ἐφ’ ἱπποδάμοισιν ἐγείρομεν ὀξὺν Ἄρηα.
sentences.tr:
all’ athrooi hormēthentes
Trōsin eph’ hippodamoisin egeiromen oxyn Arēa.
sentences.l:
but all together, having set out,
against the horse-taming Trojans let us rouse sharp Ares.”
sentences.i: but let us all set out together and rouse keen battle against the Trojans, tamers of horses.”
sentences.n: This unit begins in the middle of line 236. The speech ends on a call to act at once. ἀλλά ‘but’ turns from the one who is left behind to the group as a whole. ἀθρόοι ‘all together’ is the house rendering. ὁρμηθέντες is the aorist passive participle of ὁρμάω ‘set out, rush’. ἐγείρομεν is a short-vowel subjunctive, ‘let us rouse’, after ἀλλά; the same form is a plain present indicative at 4.352, but here the call to act makes it a hortative. Τρωσὶν ἐφ’ ἱπποδάμοισιν ‘against the horse-taming Trojans’ is the stock epithet, translated every time. ὀξὺν Ἄρηα ‘sharp Ares’ is a formula: Ares stands for war, so the sense is ‘keen battle’.
